summary: No new orders: Nvidia's results were good but the market's response so far is small, and the S&P 500 fund ended Tuesday almost exactly on the line at which I would sell it, so the $249 in cash stays put rather than being added to a holding that could be cut tomorrow.
thesis:
Where the account stands. At the end of Tuesday 17 November it was worth $977.08 against $963.98 for the benchmark, $1,000 left in an S&P 500 fund. Both are down; the account has lost less because a quarter of it is in cash and the rest leans away from the giant technology companies. Five trading days is too short to call that lead skill.

What has happened since the last decision:

- Tuesday was another broad down day. The S&P 500 fund SPY fell 1.01%, the Dow fund DIA 1.62%, the small company fund IWM 1.43% and the equal-weight fund RSP 1.45%. Falling shares outnumbered rising ones by nearly three to one. Unlike the earlier days, the selling was no longer confined to technology: RSP fell more than SPY, and health care (XLV) fell 1.41%. October retail sales rose 0.2% after 0.8% in September, a soft number, and import prices rose 1.1% for a second month, which keeps inflation worries alive.
- Nvidia reported after the close. Revenue was $115.8 billion, up 103% on a year earlier and above the roughly $109 billion expected, and it forecast about $130 billion for the current quarter, also above expectations. The board said it will not bring back its former chief executive; the finance chief stays in charge for now. There are reports that the securities regulator is looking into the circumstances of his exit. The shares rose about 1% to 3% after hours and before the open, after four days of falls.
- This morning futures pointed to the S&P 500 opening about 0.1% to 0.3% higher, the Nasdaq 100 about 0.5% to 0.8% higher and the Dow close to flat or slightly lower. The 10-year Treasury yield was about 5.10%, a touch lower. US crude was near $84. Housing figures come out this morning and the notes of the Federal Reserve's October meeting this afternoon. Markets still expect the Fed to raise rates on 9 December.

Each holding judged against what I wrote when I bought it:

1. SPY ended at $732.44. The line for selling it is a day ending below its 200-day average, which is now $732.30. It is above that line by 14 cents, about 0.02%. The rule has not been triggered, so I keep it, and I am not moving the line. If SPY ends any day below its 200-day average, the next decision sells it. Today's futures suggest it opens a little higher, but that settles nothing.

2. RSP ended at $215.76, 0.4% above its 50-day average ($214.96), the level that would send it back into SPY. Over 20 trading days it is flat while SPY is down 4.8%, so the reason for owning it, that the average company would hold up better than the giants, is still working. But it is very close to its line. If it ends a day below its 50-day average, the next decision acts on it; with SPY also near its own line, the likely move then is to hold the proceeds in cash rather than switch into SPY.

3. XLV ended at $185.24, about 2.7% below what I paid and 5.4% above its 50-day average ($175.70). The 8% loss limit is about $174. Nothing in the news concerns drug pricing or insurance policy. Keep, and do not add: it is still 15% above its 200-day average.

4. Cash, $249 (25%). The last decision said that if Nvidia's results were well received, the likely move would be to put most of the cash into SPY. The results passed, but I am not doing that, for two reasons. First, the reception is modest: a 1% to 3% rise in Nvidia and a fraction of a percent in the S&P 500 futures after four straight down days is not a turn, and Tuesday showed selling spreading beyond technology. Second, SPY sits exactly on the line at which I would sell it. Buying more of a holding I may be required to sell tomorrow would only add fees. The original conditions for spending the cash early, results passed and SPY back above its 50-day average (now about $763), are not met: SPY is 4% below that level. The end date stays as written: fully invested no later than the first trading day after the Fed decision of 9 December. If SPY breaks its 200-day average, the cash is the account's protection; if it recovers above its 50-day average first, the cash goes in then.

I looked at moving the cash into a Treasury bill fund (SGOV) for the three weeks; the interest would be about the same as the fees to get in and out, so it stays as plain cash. I looked at consumer staples (XLP) as shelter again; it is already held inside RSP, fell 1.23% on Tuesday along with everything else, and buying it now would mean two rounds of fees for a short stay.

This is not the first decision of the month, so there is no monthly review. The first is due at the start of December.
risks: If the market takes Nvidia's results as the end of the technology sell-off, the giant companies could rebound quickly and the benchmark would gain on this account, which holds less technology and keeps a quarter in cash. If the selling continues, SPY will cross below its 200-day average and RSP below its 50-day average within a day, and the account will have to sell at lower prices; the cash softens that but does not prevent it. Health care is still well above its long-run average and fell with the market on Tuesday. The Fed's meeting notes this afternoon and a likely rate increase on 9 December could push long-term interest rates higher still. Futures and pre-market prices quoted here can change by the open, and some news pages could not be read in full this morning.
